title: Recognize the source before interpreting it

sourceWindow.translation: In the beginning God created
sourceWindow.context: This is the opening verse of the Torah, presented as a verse rather than a rabbinic case or discussion.

teachingMove: Before asking what a source means, name its family. Genre tells you what kinds of questions will help.
prompt: Which first move best orients you to this source?

choices.text: Identify it as a Torah verse, then notice its speaker, action, and setting.
Treat it as a final halakhic ruling and look immediately for a practical verdict.
Treat it as a Gemara debate and divide its words into challenge and response.

feedback.correct: Yes. Naming the source family gives you the right reading moves without asking you to know everything first.
feedback.incorrect: Start with genre: this is a Torah verse. Then ask verse-shaped questions about speaker, action, scene, and repeated language.

evidencePreview: I can recognize a Jewish source family before I interpret it.

title: Find the case before the ruling

sourceWindow.translation: From when may one recite Shema in the evenings?
sourceWindow.context: The Mishnah opens by defining a concrete case: the permitted time for evening Shema.

teachingMove: A Mishnah often becomes readable when you separate the situation being governed from the ruling about it.
prompt: What is the case this Mishnah asks you to locate?

choices.text: A person needs to know when the evening window for reciting Shema begins.
A person needs to decide who first composed every word of the prayer.
A person needs to reconstruct the political history of the Second Temple.

feedback.correct: Right. The case is the evening recitation window; the following positions define its boundary.
feedback.incorrect: Return to the opening question. The case is practical and bounded: when evening Shema may begin.

evidencePreview: I can identify the case a Mishnah is governing.

title: Read a citation as an address

sourceWindow.translation: Rashi on Genesis 1:1
sourceWindow.context: A citation is an address: it names a work, sometimes a commentator, and an exact location.

teachingMove: Read a citation like an address — the work, then the chapter and verse or page, and who is speaking.
prompt: What does the citation “Rashi on Genesis 1:1” point you to?

choices.text: A prayer that is recited before studying the book of Genesis.
Rashi's commentary on the first verse of the book of Genesis.
The opening mishnah of a Talmudic tractate named Genesis.

feedback.correct: Right — the citation names a commentator (Rashi) and the exact verse (Genesis 1:1) he is explaining.
feedback.incorrect: Read the citation as an address: it names a commentator and the verse he explains, not a prayer or a tractate.

evidencePreview: I can read a simple source citation and say what it points to.

title: Tell the source apart from its commentary

sourceWindow.hebrew: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ
sourceWindow.translation: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth
sourceWindow.context: In a printed Chumash the Torah verse sits in the center; Rashi's words printed around it are a later explanation.

teachingMove: Before trusting a reading, ask which words are the source itself and which are a commentator explaining it.
prompt: On the page, which is the source and which is the commentary?

choices.text: The Torah verse is the source; Rashi's words beside it are later commentary.
Rashi's comment is the source, and the Torah verse explains Rashi.
The verse and Rashi were written together by the same author.

feedback.correct: Yes. The verse is the primary source; a commentator like Rashi writes centuries later to explain it.
feedback.incorrect: The Torah verse is the source. Rashi lived far later and writes to explain the verse, not the reverse.

evidencePreview: I can tell a source apart from the commentary printed around it.

title: Anchor a Hebrew line on a word you know

sourceWindow.hebrew: וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר וַיְהִי אוֹר
sourceWindow.translation: And God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light
sourceWindow.context: The word וַיֹּאמֶר, “and He said,” opens many verses in the Torah's creation account.

teachingMove: Anchor a Hebrew line by finding one word you can recognize, then read outward from it.
prompt: Which recurring Hebrew word anchors this verse as an act of divine speech?

choices.text: וַיֹּאמֶר — “and He said,” marking that God is speaking.
אֶרֶץ — “land,” naming where the action happens.
לַיְלָה — “night,” setting the time of the verse.

feedback.correct: Right. וַיֹּאמֶר, “and He said,” is the anchor — it recurs through creation and signals divine speech.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the word that means “and He said”: וַיֹּאמֶר. The other two words do not appear in this verse.

evidencePreview: I can notice a familiar Hebrew word and use it to anchor my reading.

title: Read repeated language as a signal

sourceWindow.translation: And God saw that it was good
sourceWindow.context: This phrase repeats after several stages of creation in Genesis 1.

teachingMove: When a phrase repeats, treat the repetition as a signal that the text wants you to notice a pattern.
prompt: What does the repetition of “And God saw that it was good” signal?

choices.text: A deliberate refrain marking each stage of creation as good.
A scribal mistake that accidentally copied the same line twice.
A disagreement between two rabbis about the correct wording.

feedback.correct: Yes. The repeated refrain is a pattern — it frames each stage of creation as good, on purpose.
feedback.incorrect: Repetition here is deliberate, not an error or a dispute. The refrain marks each creation stage as good.

evidencePreview: I can recognize repeated language and read it as a deliberate signal.

title: Name the speaker and the scene

sourceWindow.hebrew: וַיִּקְרָא ה׳ אֱלֹהִים אֶל הָאָדָם וַיֹּאמֶר לוֹ אַיֶּכָּה
sourceWindow.translation: And the LORD God called to the man and said to him, “Where are you?”
sourceWindow.context: This verse comes just after the man and woman eat from the tree in the garden.

teachingMove: Before interpreting a narrative verse, name who is speaking and where the scene takes place.
prompt: Who is speaking, and in what scene?

choices.text: God is speaking to the man in the garden, after the eating.
The man is calling out to God to ask where God has gone.
Moses is speaking to the whole people at Mount Sinai.

feedback.correct: Right. God calls to the man in the garden; the scene follows the eating from the tree.
feedback.incorrect: Read the speaker: “the LORD God called to the man.” God is speaking, in the garden, not Moses at Sinai.

evidencePreview: I can identify the speaker and the scene in a Tanakh verse.

title: Tell narrative from command

sourceWindow.translation: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy
sourceWindow.context: This line appears among the Ten Commandments given at Sinai.

teachingMove: Ask whether a verse is telling what happened (narrative) or telling you to do something (command).
prompt: Is this verse narrative or command?

choices.text: A command — it instructs the listener to remember and sanctify the Sabbath.
A narrative — it reports that the people once remembered the Sabbath.
A question — it asks whether the Sabbath ought to be kept.

feedback.correct: Yes. “Remember… to keep it holy” is an instruction — a command, not a report of past events.
feedback.incorrect: The verb “Remember… keep it holy” instructs the listener. That makes it a command, not narrative or a question.

evidencePreview: I can tell whether a Torah verse is narrative or command.

title: Locate the ruling in a Mishnah

sourceWindow.translation: Until midnight — the words of Rabbi Eliezer
sourceWindow.context: After asking from when the evening Shema may be recited, the Mishnah states a limit.

teachingMove: Once you have found the case a Mishnah governs, look for the ruling: the answer or limit it sets.
prompt: What ruling does this line state?

choices.text: The evening Shema may be recited until midnight.
Rabbi Eliezer composed the words of the Shema prayer.
Reciting the Shema in the evening is entirely forbidden.

feedback.correct: Right. The ruling is a time limit: evening Shema may be said until midnight, per Rabbi Eliezer.
feedback.incorrect: The ruling is the limit the Mishnah sets — “until midnight” — not who authored the prayer or a prohibition.

evidencePreview: I can identify the ruling a Mishnah states.

title: Spot a dispute between positions

sourceWindow.hebrew: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים... וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים כָּל אָדָם קוֹרֵא כְּדַרְכּוֹ
sourceWindow.translation: Beit Shammai say… and Beit Hillel say: everyone may recite in their usual way
sourceWindow.context: The Mishnah records how one should be positioned when reciting the evening Shema.

teachingMove: When two names or schools are each introduced by “say,” expect a dispute — two positions on one question.
prompt: What tells you this Mishnah records a dispute?

choices.text: Two schools, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, each give a different ruling.
A single agreed ruling is stated by everyone together.
It tells a story of a debate that was never resolved into positions.

feedback.correct: Yes. “Beit Shammai say… Beit Hillel say” presents two opposing positions — the signature of a dispute.
feedback.incorrect: Two schools are each introduced with “say,” giving opposing rulings. That structure is a dispute.

evidencePreview: I can identify a dispute between positions in a Mishnah.

title: Find the Gemara's question

sourceWindow.translation: On what does the tanna stand, that he teaches “from when”?
sourceWindow.context: The Gemara opens by questioning why the Mishnah begins with the word “from when.”

teachingMove: Find the Gemara's question first — it usually asks why the Mishnah said what it said.
prompt: What move is the Gemara making here?

choices.text: It is asking a question: why does the Mishnah begin this way?
It is issuing a final legal ruling on when to recite Shema.
It is praising the tanna for his careful wording.

feedback.correct: Right. The Gemara is questioning the Mishnah's opening — “on what does the tanna stand?” is a question.
feedback.incorrect: This is a question, not a ruling or praise: the Gemara asks why the Mishnah opens with “from when.”

evidencePreview: I can identify a question the Gemara is asking.

title: Find the Gemara's answer

sourceWindow.translation: He stands on a verse
sourceWindow.context: In answer to why the Mishnah begins with “from when,” the Gemara says the tanna relies on a verse.

teachingMove: After the question, look for the answer — often a short phrase that resolves what was asked.
prompt: What does this short phrase do in the sugya?

choices.text: It answers the question: the tanna is relying on a verse of the Torah.
It raises a brand-new, unrelated question about prayer.
It records a sage refusing to answer the question at all.

feedback.correct: Yes. “He stands on a verse” answers the question — the Mishnah's wording rests on Scripture.
feedback.incorrect: This phrase resolves the question: the tanna relies on a verse. It is an answer, not a new question.

evidencePreview: I can identify an answer the Gemara gives to its question.

title: Hear a challenge coming

sourceWindow.translation: They raise an objection
sourceWindow.context: The word מֵיתִיבֵי signals that a source is about to be cited against a stated position.

teachingMove: Learn the signal words: מֵיתִיבֵי warns you a challenge is coming, not agreement.
prompt: What does the word מֵיתִיבֵי signal is coming next?

choices.text: A challenge: a source is cited to object to the stated position.
A proof that everyone already agrees with the position.
A blessing recited before continuing to study.

feedback.correct: Right. מֵיתִיבֵי, “they raise an objection,” signals an incoming challenge from a cited source.
feedback.incorrect: מֵיתִיבֵי means “they object.” It flags a challenge to the position, not agreement or a blessing.

evidencePreview: I can recognize a Gemara challenge from its signal word.

title: Separate the verse from the ruling it grounds

sourceWindow.translation: And you shall speak of them… when you lie down and when you rise up
sourceWindow.context: From this verse the halakha derives an obligation to recite the Shema evening and morning.

teachingMove: Keep the source verse and the practical ruling separate: the verse is Scripture; the ruling is what the law derives from it.
prompt: Which is the source, and which is the derived halakhic ruling?

choices.text: The verse is the source; “recite Shema morning and evening” is the derived ruling.
“Recite Shema twice daily” is itself the Torah verse, word for word.
The verse and the practice of reciting Shema are unrelated.

feedback.correct: Yes. The verse is Scripture; the obligation to say Shema morning and evening is the ruling derived from it.
feedback.incorrect: The verse (“when you lie down and rise up”) is the source; the twice-daily obligation is derived from it, not identical to it.

evidencePreview: I can distinguish a Torah source from the halakhic ruling derived from it.

title: See the line a halakha draws

sourceWindow.translation: From when may one recite the Shema in the evenings?
sourceWindow.context: The Mishnah fixes a practical window: when the obligation begins and when it ends.

teachingMove: Notice where a halakha draws a line in time or space — the boundary is often the practical heart of the rule.
prompt: What kind of boundary is this Mishnah drawing?

choices.text: A boundary in time: the window during which evening Shema may be said.
A boundary of persons: which people are allowed to pray at all.
A boundary of place: the only city where Shema may be recited.

feedback.correct: Right. The rule sets a time boundary — the window for evening Shema — which is where the practice lives.
feedback.incorrect: “From when… in the evenings” fixes a time window, not a limit on who may pray or where.

evidencePreview: I can recognize the practical boundary a halakha draws.

title: Find the verse a Midrash is reading

sourceWindow.translation: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness
sourceWindow.context: A midrash notices the plural “let us make” and asks whom God is addressing.

teachingMove: First find the exact word or verse a midrash is reading before you weigh what it says about it.
prompt: Which verse is this midrash reading?

choices.text: Genesis 1:26 — “Let us make man,” with its striking plural.
The Shema, “Hear O Israel,” from the book of Deuteronomy.
The splitting of the sea in the book of Exodus.

feedback.correct: Right. The midrash is reading Genesis 1:26 — the plural “let us make man” is what it questions.
feedback.incorrect: The midrash quotes “Let us make man” — Genesis 1:26 — not the Shema or the Exodus story.

evidencePreview: I can identify which verse a Midrash is reading.

title: Name the midrashic move

sourceWindow.translation: Let us make man
sourceWindow.context: The midrash fastens on the plural verb “let us make” and draws meaning from it.

teachingMove: Name the interpretive move: a midrash often builds meaning from an odd word, a plural, or an extra letter.
prompt: What interpretive move is the midrash making?

choices.text: It reads meaning into the plural “let us,” asking whom God consults.
It counts how many times the chapter is recited in daily prayer.
It simply translates the verse into Aramaic with no comment.

feedback.correct: Yes. The move is to notice the unusual plural “let us make” and derive meaning from it.
feedback.incorrect: The midrash builds on the odd plural “let us make.” That noticing is the interpretive move.

evidencePreview: I can name a midrashic interpretive move.

title: Find the central claim

sourceWindow.hebrew: אִם אֵין אֲנִי לִי, מִי לִי? וּכְשֶׁאֲנִי לְעַצְמִי, מָה אֲנִי?
sourceWindow.translation: If I am not for myself, who is for me? And when I am only for myself, what am I?
sourceWindow.context: Hillel states two short lines held in tension with each other.

teachingMove: In a text of Jewish thought, find the central claim before the examples or objections.
prompt: What is Hillel's central claim?

choices.text: A person must take responsibility for themselves and also for others.
A person should care only about themselves and no one else.
A person should never make a decision without waiting a full year.

feedback.correct: Right. Hillel holds both lines together: care for yourself, but do not live for yourself alone.
feedback.incorrect: The two lines balance each other — self-responsibility and responsibility to others — not selfishness or delay.

evidencePreview: I can identify the central claim in a text of Jewish thought.

title: Recognize the shape of a blessing

sourceWindow.hebrew: כָּל בְּרָכָה שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ שֵׁם וּמַלְכוּת אֵינָהּ בְּרָכָה
sourceWindow.translation: Any blessing that lacks God's name and kingship is not a blessing
sourceWindow.context: The Talmud defines what every blessing must contain: God's name and a mention of divine kingship.

teachingMove: Learn the fixed shape of a blessing — “Blessed are You, LORD… King of the universe” — so you can recognize it anywhere.
prompt: According to this rule, what must a blessing contain?

choices.text: God's name and a mention of kingship (…LORD… King of the universe).
The name of the person who is reciting the blessing.
The exact date and time at which it is being said.

feedback.correct: Right. A blessing needs God's name and kingship — the fixed frame “Blessed are You, LORD… King of the universe.”
feedback.incorrect: The rule names two required parts: God's name and kingship, not the speaker's name or the date.

evidencePreview: I can recognize the fixed structure of a blessing.

title: Sort praise, request, and thanks

sourceWindow.translation: We give thanks to You
sourceWindow.context: This line opens the Modim paragraph of the Amidah, one of prayer's three basic kinds.

teachingMove: Sort prayer into its basic moves: praise of God, requests, and thanks — each has its own tone.
prompt: Which move of prayer is “We give thanks to You”?

choices.text: Thanks — gratitude for what has been given.
Request — asking God for something not yet received.
Complaint — protesting against a hardship.

feedback.correct: Right. “We give thanks to You” is the prayer's move of thanks, distinct from praise or request.
feedback.incorrect: “We give thanks” expresses gratitude — the move of thanks, not a request or a complaint.

evidencePreview: I can distinguish praise, request, and thanks in prayer.

title: Order the layers of the canon

sourceWindow.hebrew: מֹשֶׁה קִבֵּל תּוֹרָה מִסִּינַי וּמְסָרָהּ לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ
sourceWindow.translation: Moses received the Torah from Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua
sourceWindow.context: The Mishnah opens by tracing a chain of transmission across the generations.

teachingMove: Hold a rough timeline: Torah, then Mishnah, then Gemara, then the Rishonim — earlier layers are quoted by later ones.
prompt: Which ordering of the canon is correct, earliest to latest?

choices.text: Torah, then Mishnah, then Gemara, then the Rishonim.
The Rishonim, then Gemara, then Mishnah, then Torah.
Gemara, then Torah, then the Rishonim, then Mishnah.

feedback.correct: Right. Torah comes first, then the Mishnah, then the Gemara, then the medieval Rishonim.
feedback.incorrect: The canon builds forward in time: Torah, Mishnah, Gemara, Rishonim — later layers quote earlier ones.

evidencePreview: I can place Torah, Mishnah, Gemara, and Rishonim in broad order.

title: Sort law, custom, value, and memory

sourceWindow.translation: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy
sourceWindow.context: Around a single practice like Shabbat sit different kinds of claim: law, custom, value, and memory.

teachingMove: When you meet a practice, sort the claim: is it halakha (obligation), minhag (custom), a value, or a memory?
prompt: “Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy” is stated here as which kind of claim?

choices.text: Halakha — a binding obligation commanded in the Torah.
Minhag — a local custom that varies by community.
A personal memory with no obligation attached to it.

feedback.correct: Right. Commanded in the Torah, keeping Shabbat is halakha — a binding obligation, not merely a custom or memory.
feedback.incorrect: As a Torah commandment, this is halakha — an obligation — not a custom (minhag) or a private memory.

evidencePreview: I can distinguish halakha, minhag, value, and memory.

title: Return to the work after a gap

sourceWindow.hebrew: לֹא עָלֶיךָ הַמְּלָאכָה לִגְמֹר, וְלֹא אַתָּה בֶן חוֹרִין לִבָּטֵל מִמֶּנָּה
sourceWindow.translation: It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you free to desist from it
sourceWindow.context: Rabbi Tarfon frames learning as ongoing work you return to, not a task you must complete at once.

teachingMove: After a missed day, return to the work rather than abandoning it — consistency beats completion.
prompt: What does this teaching suggest after you miss a day of learning?

choices.text: Return to the work; you need not finish it all, only not abandon it.
Since you cannot finish it, it is better to stop learning entirely.
You must begin the entire curriculum over again from the start.

feedback.correct: Right. You are not required to finish, but you are not free to quit — so you return and continue.
feedback.incorrect: The teaching says not to desist: you return to the work after a gap rather than quitting or restarting everything.

evidencePreview: I can recover after missing a learning day.

title: Carry a skill into a new source

sourceWindow.translation: Who is wise? One who learns from every person
sourceWindow.context: Ben Zoma defines wisdom as the ability to learn from any source, not only familiar ones.

teachingMove: Take a move you learned in one place and try it on a new, unfamiliar source — that is transfer.
prompt: How does this teaching describe a skilled learner?

choices.text: One who can carry learning into every new person and source.
One who learns from only a single approved teacher.
One who memorizes facts but never applies them elsewhere.

feedback.correct: Right. Learning from every person is transfer — carrying a skill into new and unfamiliar sources.
feedback.incorrect: Ben Zoma praises learning from everyone — applying skills to new sources — not sticking to one teacher or rote memory.

evidencePreview: I can transfer one learned skill to a new source.
